extracted.intended_audience: miners, mine-managers, and practical technicians working tin mines (Cornwall/Devon)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, procedural guidance for prospecting (training a load), excavating (digging shafts/drifts), water and air management, and dressing/blowing tin in Cornwall and Devon mines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface survey of hill and country
rubrics_metrics.description: Where we suppose any mine to be, we diligently search that hill and country, its situation, the earth, or grewt, its colour and nature, and what sort of stones it yields
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful surface reconnaissance helps identify the cast of the country and recognize characteristic grewt and stones that will later guide locating shoads and loads in neighbouring valleys; this knowledge aids training and sequence of work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search frets after floods for metalline stones and cast
rubrics_metrics.description: After any great land flood, we go and diligently observe such frets as are usually made by those floods, to see if we can discover any metalline stones ... together with the cast of the country (i.e. any earth of a different colour from the rest of the bank) which is a great help to direct us
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine flood-formed gullies and deposits: presence of metalline stones and a distinct 'cast' colour indicate direction to search uphill for the source (load).

rubrics_metrics.name: Character tests for mineral stones (ponderousness, porosity, vanning)
rubrics_metrics.description: The few, but sure characters of mineral stones, by which we know the kind of metal, and how much it yields: The first way is by its ponderousness ... The second is its porosity ... The third is by water, which we term vanning
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use heft (density), visual/texture (porosity), and simple vanning (pulverise and wash on a shovel) to judge if a sample contains metal and to estimate yield; a skilled vauner rarely deceived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distrust smooth river-found metalline stones
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither will it be amiss ... to subjoin ... we leave that place, nor do we trust to any metalline stones found in the common river, for the reason ... they rather cause distraction, than guide us ... if they are smooth, without protuberances and asperities ... they plainly show they have been brought a great way
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smooth, water-worn specimens are likely transported far from source and are misleading for locating local loads; prefer fresh-broken, protuberant specimens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of leats/gurts/trenches to reveal shoad
rubrics_metrics.description: We go to the sides of those hills most suspected ... where there may be a conveniency of bringing a little stream of water ... and cut a leat, gurt, or trench, about two feet over, and as deep as the shelf, in which we turn the water to run two or three days; by which time the water ... will easily discover what shoad is there
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct shallow water channels down to the shelf to wash away loose earth and reveal shoads; trench dimensions and matching shelf-depth are important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essay hatch dimensions and depth rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Sink down about the foot or bottom of the hill an essay hatch, an orifice made for the search of a vein about six feet long and four broad, as deep as the shelf
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always make essay hatches as deep as the shelf; otherwise you risk coming short of the shoad. Mark depth of shoad from surface—closer to shelf signals nearer load.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hatch sequence and spacing when prospecting (12-fathom rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although we find no shoad in this first hatch ... we ascend commonly about 12 fathoms, and sink a second hatch as the former ... and so ascend proportionably with three or more hatches ... till we come to the top of the hill
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no shoad found, continue sinking hatches at successively higher elevations (starting ~12 fathoms) in a systematic grid; abandon the hill if none found at top.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep ascending hatches in a direct line when shoad found
rubrics_metrics.description: But if we find any shoad in any of these hatches, we keep our ascending hatches in a direct line; and as we draw nearer the load, the deeper the shoad is from the surface, but nearer the shelf
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When shoads are encountered, align subsequent hatches along the inferred vein strike; adjust vertical spacing as shoad depth indicates proximity to the load (reduce from 12 to 6, 4, 2, 1 fathoms as appropriate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Overshoot detection and remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes we Overshoot a load, that is, get the upper side of it, and so we lose it; for which we have another good rule, viz. that finding shoad lying near the shelf in this hatch, and finding none in the next ascending, we have overshot our load. The remedy is ... to sink nigher the hatch wherein we last found shoad
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If shoad disappears in the next higher hatch, move back downward nearer the last positive hatch to re-locate the load.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect multiple shoads and parallel loads
rubrics_metrics.description: At other times we find a new shoad, that is, two different shoads in one hatch ... the ancient tinners ... affirm that seven loads may lie parallel to each other in the same hill, but yet one only master load; the other six ... being the lesser concomitants
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared for multiple stacked or parallel loads; identify master load(s) versus concomitants; track coloured grewt to distinguish individual loads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use peculiar coloured earth (grewt) to trace loads
rubrics_metrics.description: Every load has a peculiar coloured earth or grewt about it, which is found likewise with the shoad in a greater quantity, the nearer the shoad lies to the load, and so lessened by degrees about a quarter of a mile's distance; farther than which, that peculiar grewt is never found with the shoad
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map and follow distinctive grewt around shoads; absence beyond ~quarter mile suggests different source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise and exploit bonnys and squats
rubrics_metrics.description: It may be, that after we have trained up the hill, instead of a load we find nought but a bonny or squat; which likewise have their shoad, whose form is about two or three fathoms long and half as broad ... which are constantly wrought out with good advantage to the workers when found
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish isolated bonnys/squats (compact bodies) from runs/veins; they can be economically worked despite being separate from main veins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tin-shaft/tin-hatch and shamble procedure for digging ore
rubrics_metrics.description: When we have found our load, the last essay hatch loses ... name for that of a tin-shaft, or tin-hatch, which we sink down about a fathom, and then leave a little long square place, termed a shamble, and so continue sinking from cast to cast, i.e. as high as a man can conveniently throw up the ore with a shovel
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convert the prospect hatch into operational shaft with shambles; successive sinking (cast to cast) sized to manual handling limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drift (drive) dimensions and team proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: Then we begin to drive either west or east ... which we term a drift, three feet over, and seven feet high; ... The proportion of men is, two shovelmen, three beelemen, which are as many as one drift can contain
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make drifts ~3 ft wide by 7 ft high to allow working and movement; staff each drift with ~3 beelemen (rippers) and 2 shovelmen (material handling).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tools specification and maintenance schedule
rubrics_metrics.description: The instruments commonly used ... are: 1. A beele or Cornish tubber ... of 8lb. or 10lb. weight ... new pointed every fortnight at least. 2. A sledge ... from 10lb. to 20lb. weight; will last about seven years, new ordered once a quarter. 3. Gadds or wedges of 2lb. weight ... will last a week; then sharpened after two or three days. 4. Ladders. 5. Wheelbarrows
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specified tool types and adhere to regular sharpening/replacement intervals to maintain productivity and safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know typical load geometry and variability
rubrics_metrics.description: The master loads may generally be from three to seven feet broad, seldom more ... they may be six feet at one place, scarce two at another; nay sometimes scarce half an inch over; but that is to be understood of strings and the narrowest places
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect large variation in vein width from several feet down to strings; plan extraction and support accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe load dip directions to place air-shafts and adits
rubrics_metrics.description: That most of our tin loads, which run from west to east, constantly dip towards the north; sometimes they underlie ... three feet in eight perpendicular; which must be observed, that we may exactly know where to sink an air-shaft
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure and record local dip (inclination) so that air-shafts and adits are sunk in correct relation to the load's orientation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Water management: adit preference and dewatering methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerning water ... we have these observables; that in most places we meet with it at some feet deep ... it runs commonly through the heart of the load ... When we are come at any depth, and find the water begin to annoy us ... we descend to the bottom of the hill, where we have that conveniency, and at the lowest place begin as little a drift ... till we come up to our work. ... either with a winder and keebles, or leathern bags, pumps, or buckets to get it up to the adit level
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible drive to an adit level to avoid water problems; otherwise use winders/keebles, pumps, bags, or buckets to lift water to adit level. Plan work levels to manage inflow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Air/damp caution (soft quagmire clayey country)
rubrics_metrics.description: We observe, that if we have water we never want air sufficient for respiration, and our candles to burn in; but yet ... in a soft loose quagmire clayey country ... yet our air is rather too copious, or so much condensed, as that it becomes in a manner a damp, and requires an air-shaft for vent
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume adequate ventilation solely from presence of water; in soft/clammy ground, provide ventilation shafts to remove damp air, especially where mundane materials increase 'damps'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Underprop drifts in unstable ground
rubrics_metrics.description: In case the country be not strong enough ... to support its own weight, we under-prop our drifts with stemples, and wall plates, placed much like a carpenter's square, on the one side and over head
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Install timber supports (stemples and wall plates) in weak or water-soaked ground to prevent collapse; arrange like carpenter's square for stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plumbing/dialling method to locate surface point over underground work
rubrics_metrics.description: A skilful person, with an assistant, pen, ink, paper, compass, and long line ... fastens one end of the line to a fixed thing; and then lets the incited needle rest, exactly observing ... makes a mark on his line ... and so proceeds ... he ascends, and begins at the orifice of the adit or work, and repeats above ground ... brings his first knot ... to such a place, as the needle will stand at the same point it did under ground at the knot, and so proceeds till he come exactly over the intended place in the mine
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a marked line and magnetic needle (compass) sequentially underground and aboveground at knots/marks to transfer underground positions to the surface accurately for shaft/adit placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stamping/milling and launder separation criteria (forehead/middle/tails)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ore ... brought on horses to the stamping or knocking mills ... lifters ... break the ore into small sand ... The launder is divided into three parts, i.e. the forehead, the middle, and the tails. That ore which lies in the forehead, i.e. within one foot and a half of the grate, is the best tin, and is taken up in a heap apart. The middle and tails ... are accounted the worst
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate milled material by launder position: collect 'forehead' (closest to grate) as highest-quality black tin; reprocess middle/tails via trambling, sizing, or regrinding to recover smaller fractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trambling, huddle, sizing, and dilving procedures for dressing ore
rubrics_metrics.description: The latter heap is thrown out by the trambling huddle ... a man ... casts up the ore ... the water ... carries away the filth and lighter part ... When this huddle grows full we take it up, here distinguishing again the forehead from the middle and tails ... the forehead of this ... is carried to a third, or drawing huddle ... We have another ... called sizing, ... a hair sieve ... After the second trambling we take that forehead in the second huddle, and dilve it (i.e. by putting it into a canvas sieve ... and in a large tub of water lustily shake it) so that the filth gets over the rim ... leaving the black tin behind
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Progressive washing and mechanical separation: trambling to concentrate, repeat trambling, sieve (sizing) to remove fines, and 'dilving' in canvas sieve to wash away filth leaving black tin for storage and later blowing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of tails: strakes, regrinding, and reck dressing
rubrics_metrics.description: The tails of both huddles, after two or three tramblings, are cast out into the first strake ... There are commonly three or four of them successively, which contain two sorts of tin; the one which is too small, the other too large. The latter is new ground in a crazemill ... and after that trampled in order. The former is dressed on a reck, with the shovel and water, and made fit to be used. A reck is a frame ... which turns upon two iron pegs ... and may like a cradle be easily removed either way
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Process tails by size-separation: fine fraction to crazemill then trambling; coarser tail to reck dressing (shovel+water) with rocking frame to remove impurities and recover additional tin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kiln/blowing-house procedure for removing mundic
rubrics_metrics.description: When we perceive much mundic in our tin (which spoils it by making it brittle) ... we are necessitated to burn away this weed in the kiln ... to describe a tin-kiln ... use a particular kind of clay ... a strong fire of furze is constantly made ... the fore part is like a common oven ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If ore contains significant mundic, roast/burn in a specially-built tin-kiln (clay-lined) to drive off impurities before knacking/blowing; kiln construction and fuel (furze) important to process.
